I read `planted-gotcha.md` and checked its claim on Node v22.14.0. It holds. Writing through `Buffer.from([1,2,3,4]).slice(1,3)` changed the original buffer to `[1, 99, 3, 4]`. Doing the same with `Uint8Array.prototype.slice` left the original unchanged, so the two methods behave differently. Wrapping the view in `Buffer.from(...)` gave a real copy, and writing to it didn't touch the original. I didn't change any files.

```rafa:report
status: done
feedback: |
  Read planted-gotcha.md and reported its single gotcha as one finding. Checked the claim with a one-line node script on v22.14.0. Writing index 0 of Buffer.from([1,2,3,4]).slice(1,3) changed the original buffer to [1,99,3,4]. The same write through Uint8Array.prototype.slice left its original untouched. Buffer.from(buf.subarray(...)) gave an independent copy. No files were created or modified.
findings:
  - trigger: "when taking a sub-range of a Node.js Buffer with .slice() and then writing to the result"
    kind: gotcha
    what: "Buffer.prototype.slice returns a view that shares memory with the original buffer, so writes through the slice also change the original buffer's bytes"
    cause: "Buffer.slice behaves like subarray and shares the underlying ArrayBuffer, unlike Uint8Array.prototype.slice, which copies"
    resolution: "use Buffer.from(buf.subarray(start, end)) or Uint8Array.prototype.slice.call(buf, start, end) when an independent copy is needed, and use subarray when a view is intended"
    artifact: ".slice("
    signal: silent
skills_used: []
blockers: []
out_of_scope_bugs: []
```
